It's such a pleasure to have you here at SEMA, here in Colombia,
a student investment club at Columbia Business Bowl.
And, you know, it's a pleasure really a pleasure to have you.
I know many of the students read your books, read about a lot of the things you write and, you know,
some of your YouTube videos.
And, yeah, why don't you start and then we'll get to some time later.
Okay, yeah, it's a pleasure and honor to be with you guys.
I always feel like to collaborate.
Columbia, it's hallowed ground because Ben Graham and the legacy there and Buffett being a student,
etc. So it's always wonderful to be with the students. And in the pre-Zoom era, I used to come to Bruce Greenwald's
class. And that was always a lot of fun. And maybe I can speak for maybe five or 10 minutes and
then maybe we can go to Q&A, just a little bit of a preamble, then take it from there.
I think you guys might have seen in Poffitz letter this year that last year, actually,
that he had mentioned that basically 12 ideas or 12 investments that he made for Berkshow
or 58 years were responsible for most of the outcome.
You know, these 12 decisions, you know, one of them might have been hiring Ajit Jane,
you know, the Coke investment and Amex and Cap Cities and so on and Seas Candy and so on.
And so one of the questions that comes up is, you know, I think over 58 years, my estimate is
that Buffett probably made at least three or four hundred important decisions and investing decisions.
And the hit rate, if you will, was basically like 4%, three or four percent. And it's a
three or four percent hit rate for Warren Buffett, which doesn't leave a lot of hope for the rest
of us mere models. And the question, you know, the question comes up is why
would it take even someone like Warren Buffett to find one good idea approximately every five
years, you know? And I thought about that, and I think that the five-year period might actually be almost like a
law of investing, law of value investing. And the reason is that, you know, for
for us to to get to a conviction level on a particular investment or idea that's going to move the needle means that we have
a differentiated view from most of the market. Because if our view was similar to the market,
then that would be reflected in the market. And there wouldn't be supernormal
results possible. So it's a kind of, let's say, a differentiated view that causes
the outsized returns. And I think the differentiated views, they fall into two categories. They fall into
categories where we were delusional, which means that we thought that we had a differential,
a differentiated view. But in reality, we were wrong. So we make the investment, you know,
thinking, oh, yeah, I've figured out something the market hasn't, et cetera. And
this is going to be great. And it doesn't work. So those don't count in his 12 decisions in his 12 decisions in
58 years. But he may have had probably one or two dozen of those types of situations where he had
very strong conviction, which ended up not being accurate. And the second is that you're
actually right on the money, where you've got a differentiated view,
out-sized returns. And I think one of the things that Charlie Munger used to say was that
if they had not been learning machines over that 58-year period, then their record would be a shadow
of what it actually was. In fact, nobody would even talk about them. So basically, the knowledge-based
and information and understanding about the way the world works that they started out with
58 years ago was relatively small and simple versus what they figured out over the years.
So to give you an example, Warren made an investment in Burlington Northern Railway. And first,
he made an investment in the stock where he bought, you know, some portion of the company. And then I think
maybe a few years after that, he made an offer to buy the whole company. And they
mentioned a few times that they were always negative on railroads. For most of
their career, they said that railroads were actually a poor investment. They were very regulated,
unionized, and a lot of inefficiencies. But what happened is that they noticed a few things, which
which caused them to change their mind. So one of the things that happened is the railroads over time
basically redid the bridges. They had, you know, thousands of bridges. They
they redid the bridges one by one. So it allowed double-stacked cars to go underneath them. So instead
having single stack, you could do double stack. And the second is that, you know, with diesel costs and all
of that. And the railroad also started becoming more efficient in terms of how they were running
the level of employment, the length of the trains, and so on. So basically
a tipping point came where it became much better alternative, the best alternative, which would have been
trucks. And trucks, of course, you know, we have a lot of labor and stuff. They can go anywhere and
they can go short distances. But any time you had to go long distances, then the railroad
had an advantage. Both Warren and Charlie said that they were actually late to the party.
The guy who runs Bill Gates' money at Cascade investments actually figured
it out a few years before them.
And I think even Bill Ackman may have figured it out a few years before them.
So the thing is that to go through this learning about railroads, for example, where you have a view
and then you go through a change in that view, that doesn't happen overnight.
That takes a lot of drill down to get to a conviction level and such.
So when you look at a five-year time frame, it could have easily taken them two or three months or more to really get their arms around railroads. So first, they would have had to make and made a decision that there is meat on this bone. So it's worth studying. And it's worth looking at maybe destroying one of our best loved ideas, which is railroads are stupid. And then you go into the rabbit hole of railroads, which might be two, three, four months or something. And there's also a lot of rabbit holes you go down, which
no meat on the ball. And there is no differentiated view, but the time is gone. So basically, if you think about these three-month type deep dives, in a five-year period, you can do 20 of them if you had something to do every
three months. And, you know, maybe one out of three that you think is great actually turns out to be great. So if you actually
did 20, you might have three or four that look interesting. And then one is actually a good idea.
If we look at their investment in Seas Candy, so Seas Candy was a major eye opener for Warren and Charlie.
Because the only thing Warren did in terms of interfering with management every year was that on January 1st, he changed the prices of all the candy himself.
So he would sit down with the Seas Candy price list and he would look at the inflation rate and he would like increase it at two times inflation.
And what they noticed year after the year was that there was no question.
Like they increased the prices 15% and volumes were fine.
Then they increased another 10% or 15% in the next year and volumes are still fine. And it was a huge learning for
them. I mean, there was like a huge step function learning for them to really, they were actually
in shock that there was no drop in volumes. And actually, if you think about it,
so if you know, you know, C's mostly a California story, right? It's really mostly
in California, and in this period from, you know, the 1970s till maybe, let's say
1990, let's say 1970 to 1990, that 20-year period. In that 20-year period, in that 20-year period,
California GDP probably grew at a higher rate than US GDP because it was going through so much growth.
Maybe it grew at like 4% a year or something. So the C's volume over that period, and I'm
extrapolating based on, you know, data that Berkshire's given about, you know, how many pounds are sold and all that.
Basically, sees volumes from the time they acquired till now has gone up less than 2% a year. In that period
from 70 to 90, it probably went up around 2%. Like half of California GDP growth. Part of that might
have been pushback against these huge price increases. Warren was shoving down people's
throat along with the candy. Okay. But he saw that, hey, I'm pushing this down and
it's not declining. And maybe he knew that, yeah, maybe it would have been four or five percent growth
if I didn't push the volume, if I didn't push the pricing up. But probably in that math equation,
it worked better to have higher volumes. So that learning with this, you know, annual tweaking of
C's price list eventually led to the investment in Coke. And I'm pretty sure their investment in
Coke was at least six months in the rabbit hole. Because, you know,
Munger wrote that essay, which is about how Coke becomes $2 trillion eventually and all of that. But
basically, basically, the coke investment actually took about two decades to figure out. So they
wouldn't have been able to make the coke investment in 75 or 80 or 85. It was really in the late
80s when they had enough time screwing around with Cs that they actually got a big
education on brands. And so Buffett never understood brands at all. And suddenly
there was this whole new area of this intangible moat, et cetera, which was tremendous, you know, and so then
he was able to leverage that into other consumer package goods. And even now, the Apple investment is a brand
and so the Apple investment actually is like 40 years in the making, you know,
40 or 50 years in the making. So I just wanted to share that it is very much worth
going down the rabbit holes. Because the payoffs are so big. It's also very much
okay if we hit a lot of dry wells. That's perfectly fine. You only need to get rich once. And one of these
rabbit holes could be a mother load. And so you don't need a lot of differentiated views on a lot of things.
So even like, I would say that Buffett and Munger coming up with this one dozen differentiated things.
I mean, like, insurance is a terrible business. It was a terrible business for Berkshire for 20 years
from the mid-60s to the mid-80s till Ajit Jane showed up. And when Ajit leaves the scene,
that business will shrink for them. There is no successor for that business. So they had an anomaly in
Ajit Jane showing up. And they had the second anomaly in Geico showing up,
which is more brand insurance. And so basically, even that was a situation which took
a long time to basically figure out and kind of know what you what you can do
and what's going on and so on and so on. And it worked out. So basically, I think that those are, that's
really what I wanted to share is that basically what we are looking for is we're looking for is
we're looking for anomalies. And the anomalies are not just, you know, sitting there
ready to be given to us on a platter. We have to go into different rabbit
holes. We have to decide which rabbit holes may hold some promise because there's
50,000 rabbit holes to go down. And if each one took, you know, three months, that's 200,000 quarters,
which you don't have. So you've got like maybe a hundred rabbit holes or maybe 150 rabbit holes,
if you're lucky. And got to make them count. So you don't need to make all of them count,
but you need to make some of them count. So those were some thoughts I wanted
to share with you about why even Buffett and Munger only had 12 hits in 58 years.
Right. So thank you for any insights. We'll kick off with some with some Q&A. I think,
you know, maybe to build up on your thoughts here. I think I read your book some years ago about Dando investing
and I think it doesn't sound very similar to kind of the philosophy you are talking about now.
And I wanted you to share maybe your view of, like, how your investment philosophy
philosophy has evolved during these maybe 25 years.
Well, I mean, I think the evolution I've gone through is I started out in the mid-90s as
a Mungeresque great businesses investor.
And then there was this mega bubble, dot-com bubble, 99 in 2000.
It wasn't just dot com.
It was tech and a lot of things.
In fact, most of my portfolio was tech in the 90s. And I got concerned that these valuations and numbers made no sense. I mean, we had Microsoft at, you know, 600 billion and with single digit billion cash flows. You know, 600 billion market cap, like 70 trailing earnings, like 70 times earnings or something. And I just didn't think that that was going to lead to the Holy Grail. And it turned out that that was the case. Microsoft then flatlined all the next 13 years. In fact, it didn't flatline. It was a
lost a huge portion of its value and then came back.
But basically, you held it from 99 to 2012, you basically had like zero returns.
And so in the 99, in the 99, 2000 time frame, I switched to hardcore Graham.
And the reason I switched is because that's where I was finding opportunities.
I mean, the day the NASDAQ pre, I think March 7th or March 9th, 2000,
was the day that Berkshire hit a multi-year low.
So the NASDAQ hit 5,000 for the first time in March 2000, and Berkshire went down to like, I don't know,
40,000 or something from 70,000 dropped a lot.
Literally people were selling Berkshire to buy Pets.com.
You know, that's what was going on at that time.
So basically, I thought the great businesses and the tech businesses were very high risk
at those valuations.
And so I moved to, you know, buying funeral homes at two times earnings and steel mills at three times earnings and that sort of thing. And that worked really well. And that worked really well. And what I should have done in hindsight is around 2012 or 2013, I should have switched back. Because by then, the great businesses, the valuations had come into line. You know, they'd gone through all their corrections and everything. But I had become so comfortable in the wonderful world of Ben Graham. I, I probably
was late by about five or six years.
Started to make that switch in 2018 or something.
But also in this business, just like I talked about with Warren and Charlie, you have to be a continuous learning
machine.
machine. And so on a broader basis, I think this is kind of how my journey was, you know, Munger, Graham,
Munger, Munger. You know, basically that's kind of how it went. But that would be too
simplistic. I think also what happens over that 25-year period, or 30 years almost, is that we learn a lot of things about how things work in many different places or many different industries that we didn't know. So knowledge is cumulative and so that helps as well. The Dhanddo investor, I mean, the book is like 17 years old. So clearly I've gone through some evolution since then. And yeah, if I were to rewrite it, then I would have a little different take on it.
Hey, great. Thank you. Because I know so many students want to ask some questions, I'm going to turn the stage to some questions from the students.
Manish. My name's Chris. It's a pleasure to meet you. I know you're a dear friend of Charlie's and we're going to miss them a lot. We'd love to get your take on the future Berkshire. Now that Charlie's not there.
Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, Warren has said, I think I'm almost the exact quote, is that Berkshire has been built to the blueprint of Charlie Munger and my role has been that been that of a general contractor. You know, so basically, in effect, what Warren is saying is that Charlie is the architect of Berkshire and Warren was told what to do and he executed. And then, you know, he's repeatedly to say that he would call Charlie the abominal nomad, right? Because Charlie would say no to everything.
that is that there are so many things Warren wanted to do. And of course, he was a senior partner and Charlie was a junior partner. And sometimes a senior partner
did things without talking to the junior partner, like the purchase of January, for example, which was actually not, not work well for the senior
partner for the senior partner for some time. There was some indigestion. Because the senior partner knew that the junior
partner would shut him down most of the time. And many times a junior partner would tell the senior
partner, hey, listen, we need to go big on Costco. You know, Warren has such an
aversion to paying up. And then Charlie would tell him, Warren, some things are worth paying up for.
Warren just still couldn't get that. I don't know whether you guys have heard the joke. I think
this was in the 2011 annual meeting. It's on the footage. But basically, Warren and Charlie
come back from lunch. And Warren says, you know, Charlie and I were on this
airplane that got hijacked. And Charlie, you know, he's only, can only see from one eye.
First eye that looks at the glass eye. So he's completely turned over looking at him saying,
we got like, he's asking like, we got hijacked. So, and then Warren ignores him and say, yeah,
we got hijacked. The kidnappers, oh, we've got kidnapped. And the kidnappers made a demand
of several million dollars to our families to release us. And the families basically
just keep the money. So the kidnappers get really pissed off and they tell Warren and Charlie that
not only are we not getting paid, we're going to lose two bullets now to kill you guys. So before we kill you
guys, do you have any last wish? Charlie raises his hand and says, I'd like to speak one more time
about the virtues of investing in Costco. And Warren raises his hand and says, shoot me first.
So we had the junior partner and senior partner, an interesting dynamic. And I had a lot of
discussing with Charlie about, you know, dynamic of that relationship. And I told Charlie,
I said, Charlie, Charlie, you are a type A guy. You're not a kind of guy that I see as someone who plays second
fiddled to anybody. All your other relationships with business partners, you are definitely the senior partner.
You are not only just a senior partner, you are the dictator, basically, you know,
pretty much running, you know, calling all the shots. And then here in Berkshire,
your junior. So he said to me, he said, well, Monish, it was very smart of me to become
the junior partner to Warren Buffett. And so anyway, I think they had a great relationship. I don't think
Berkshow would be anywhere near what it is today. It would not even be, in my opinion, 10% of the car market
cap, 5% of the current market cap, if there was no Charlie Munger. But I also feel
that going forward, these two guys are such iconic figures. It's kind of like the founding fathers of the
U.S. are gone, like, you know, more than 200 years back and, you know, system's still running. All the
deadlock in Washington and everything else. The system keeps running. I mean, the country's cranking and
everything's at all-time highs and everything else. So I think it will be the culture and
ethos of the place is so deeply entrenched with what Warren and Charlie
Charlie have put together, what they've preached, what is in the record, written record, and videos
videos and everything else and all the culture and the board and all that, that that I think it's like
as close to bulletproof as you can get. I don't really see any issue with Berkshire in a post-Charlie
era. I think the issue they've already faced and they will face in the future is just
size. So at some point, it'll become a dividend-paying entity or heavy buybacks
and so on. You were talking about how we only have so many rabbit holes that we can go down in a lifetime
and how we should sort of make them count. And I guess I'm wondering how do you think about which rabbit
holes are worth going down before you go down. How do you start to sort of decide what rabbit
hole to go down, knowing that some won't pan out and some will, but it only choose so many.
Yeah, I think the way to do it, the way I've done it is by being a harsh grader. So most companies
I look at in 60 seconds or less, 10 seconds. There's whole, you know, sections of value line,
which is outside circle of competence. I just take whole bunches and just not interested because,
like, I don't know anything about biotech. I don't know anything about pharma. I don't
know anything about a lot of things. So we just discard those.
Right. And then again, the idea is to reject it and move on. So it makes it past the five or 10 minutes. Then we say,
okay, let's give it an hour, see what's there for an hour. And so basically, basically, it's a gradual process
where ideas, most of them die, most of them die within five minutes. Then what's left dies within
an hour and then what's left dies within a few hours. And so once you've done a day or two
work, a lot of things have gone through your brain about, you know, it's still, like,
like, you know, Elton says, I'm still standing. The idea is still standing, you know. We can let a lot of
balls go by, and we only need to swing at the fat pitch. So if I look at Google or maybe Microsoft
10 years ago and even then felt that it was too rich in valuation, which would have been
a mistake, and I took a pass, which is probably exactly what happened.
It's not the end of the world. There's many, many more pitches coming at you. So it's okay.
Appreciate it coming by to kind of build on that question. What red flags do you look for once you start
digging to know when to stop? And then secondly, where do you see areas of opportunity today?
Yeah, I mean, I think the red flags can come from anywhere. Like, you, you have a thesis in your
head about why this thing looks exciting. And the moment you run into data that is
telling you your thesis is completely wrong, then you're done. That happens all the time. So,
for example, if publicly traded car dealerships, you know, which is a rabbit hole I'm currently in,
we don't know where the end result's going to be. But basically there's a view the market has that
in the end the world is going to be all EVs and EVs don't need much service, much parts
and these auto dealerships, these, you know, new auto dealerships have
something like 40% of their profits coming from parts and service, and that could go away.
And the second threat in that space is that EVs could be sold direct. So then what they're making
with new cars also goes away. And so if that viewpoint is accurate, new cars not being sold by
the dealership is okay because they only make like, you know, four or five percent of their
profits from new cars. New cars are so commoditized and the comparison shopping is so easy
that the margins are very low for all of them. They don't try to make money there. They know they have to
basically just be a service provider there without much margin. So my view on that is that for an OEM to go
to pass the dealer, the OEM really doesn't gain much advantage because they have to now service those
folks directly and that the very small margin that the dealer makes on the new cars is actually
being subsidized by other facets of the business. So an OE.
going direct may have more than 3, 4% in cost to, you know, sell directly. And the second
is that, you know, we get to these earlier doctors and all of that. A lot of people in the end may still want
to, you know, have a more kind of brick and motor experience with how they purchase a car, etc.
And also, some of the new V players are finding they're better off setting up a dealer network.
So I'm not sure that that particular notion carries that much weight, but it
It doesn't matter that much because the margins are so low. Then the second piece is that, you know, EVs don't need parts and service. And actually, what I found in the deep dive so far is that EVs do need a lot of parts and service. If you take a lot of parts and service. If you take out one module and replace it, it's about $7,000. And you're not
not going to go to Jiffy Lubb to do that. You know, you're going to go to the dealership and a specialized
and there's high margins and all of that. And if car gets to be 13, 14, 14 years old, it might make sense to change the
entire battery pack. The entire battery pack is like 25,000 or something, 20, 25,000. So when you look at the
And even EVs or non-EVs, they all need brakes, they all need tires, they all have a bunch
of other parts that are still going to be needing service and replacement and so on. So I concluded that actually
that's wrong, that I don't think that the parts and service goes away. And then there's a few other
aspects to some of these large players, the way they're scaling and optimizing their businesses
and so on. And so the valuations of these big guys is based on those assumptions being true,
which is that there'll be no parts in service. And in the end, these businesses
cease to exist because everyone will be selling direct. So that causes the differentiation. Now,
we'll see whether the differentiation makes it through the rabbit hole or not. But that's an example
of kind of, you know, trying to look at things in a little different way and taking it from
there. Thanks for speaking to us about a shit. 50, 70 years ago when Warren Buffett
and his mentor started investing. There was not many people looking at data, looking analytically at what's inside
companies. There's a lot of shooting from the hip, looking at the brand. Now there's so much data. Everyone's
looking at data perhaps too much sometimes. There's a massive amount of data. What's the edge you would say
that might be out there that we younger investors should look into to get that kind of step up or
that leg up against everyone else in the market.
Yeah, well, I mean, I think if we go back in history with the U.S. markets, you know, after the crash of 29
32 to 32 and then also the crash of 38, really, stock prices did not even come back to the
level of 1932 or 34 till the mid-50s. You know, like, the Dow was 400 then and 400
400 in 1954 or something. So there was a whole generation raised on the notion that,
you know, stock market is not a place to make money because it did nothing for
two decades. And of course, those are the types of conditions that set up the best conditions to do extremely
well. And the U.S. markets were an extremely good place to invest in the 50s and the 60s until we got
to Nifty 5050 and all of that. And then it became also became a really exceptional place to invest
after the 73, 74 crash. But then more recently, I think, you know, things are kind of,
and what's available. So there's always a bare market somewhere. There's always
opportunity somewhere. So if you broaden your horizons, you look at other geographies, you might find wide gaps
